---
title: "Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS)"
description: "A post-processing method that removes redundant overlapping detections while retaining high-scoring bounding boxes."
term: "Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS)"
letter: "N"
category: "Computer Vision"
difficulty: "Intermediate"
---

## Simple explanation

An object detector may produce several boxes around the same object.
Non-maximum suppression (NMS) keeps the strongest box and removes nearby
overlapping boxes that likely describe that same object.

## Technical explanation

NMS processes candidate boxes by confidence score. It selects the highest
scoring box, then suppresses remaining boxes whose intersection over union
(IoU) with it exceeds a chosen threshold. It repeats until no candidates
remain or a limit is reached.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

NMS helps convert many raw detections into a smaller set that is easier to
interpret and use. Thresholds affect the balance between duplicate boxes
and missed nearby objects, so they should be tested for the target data and
application.

## How it works

For boxes $A$ and $B$, intersection over union is
$\operatorname{IoU}(A,B)=|A\cap B|/|A\cup B|$. Standard NMS suppresses a
lower-scoring box when its IoU with a selected box exceeds the threshold.
Variants such as Soft-NMS reduce scores instead of removing boxes outright.

## Practical example

If an image detector returns three highly overlapping boxes for one car,
NMS can keep the box with the highest confidence and suppress the other
candidates. A box around a nearby second car may remain if its overlap is
below the suppression threshold.

## Common misconceptions

- NMS is post-processing, not the model's object-recognition mechanism.
- NMS can suppress a valid nearby object when boxes overlap heavily.
- The IoU threshold and score threshold have different roles and should not be confused.
